newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: New Austrian chancellor champions working class.
newsitem.headline: New Austrian chancellor champions working class.

text.p: New Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima, delivering his maiden speech to parliament, sought to woo disillusioned working class voters on Wednesday with a pledge to fight unemployment and stressed his nation's neutrality.
Deftly navigating his way through the potential minefield of defence policy, Klima said there would be no change to Austria's 41-year-old neutral status without popular support.

European Union membership and the ambitions of neighbouring former Warsaw pact states to join NATO have sparked a lively coalition debate about neutrality, which is enshrined in Austria's post-World War Two constitution.

"Austrian foreign and security policy has traditionally been determined by consensus. I will aim to pursue this line," Klima said, adding that it would be unwise to rush into a decision at a time of rapid global change.

Klima, who won his political spurs as finance minister by pushing through an unpopular austerity budget, said he would continue to keep a tight rein on public spending without losing sight of the government's duty to protect the weak.
"We must not have a blinkered or dogmatic approach. Resistance to all change is just as wrong as uncritical worship of the free market," the Social Democratic Party leader said.
"The state should be there to fulfil its duties wherever the free market fails," he continued, to enthusiastic applause from government benches.
The 49-year-old ex-industrialist formally replaced Franz Vranitzky on Tuesday as head of the coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party.

He inherited a Social Democratic Party at a post-World War Two popularity low and a coalition at loggerheads over issues ranging from the pace of privatisation to Austria's role in international defence structures.
Klima wasted no time in his first speech as chancellor to move the battle against rising unemployment to the centre of his agenda, stealing the political thunder from the opposition.

Joerg Haider's far-right Freedom Party in particular has chalked up spectacular electoral gains by playing on voters' fears of losing their jobs and homes as Austria struggles to make the grade for a single European currency.
"The fight against unemployment will be our main task in the future," Klima said.
"There is no easy answer in a world of open markets but we can try to ensure that we create new jobs to replace those that have been lost, through public and private investment."
He defended his track record as finance minister and said the government would continue to exercise fiscal discipline without squeezing ordinary people.
"Reining in the budget is not an end in itself. It makes Austria attractive to domestic and foreign investors, contributes to a stable currency and a secure job market," Klima said.
"By sticking to the 1997 budget and bringing in the necessary reforms in 1998 and 1999, we will not need to impose an austerity package on the people," he continued.
Coalition politicians were fulsome in their praise of Klima's speech. People's Party leader and Vice-Chancellor Wolfgang Schuessel spoke of a "new beginning".
Opposition parties were predictably less complimentary. The Freedom Party's Haider said: "There were plenty of words but little vision. We've heard this all before from his predecessor."
